details:
**Iphigenia at Aulis**
Agamemnon angered Artemis (often by killing a stag in her sacred grove or boasting he was a better hunter), so she stopped the winds and stranded the Greek fleet at Aulis before the Trojan War. The seer Calchas advised that Agamemnon sacrifice his daughter Iphigenia; in some versions Artemis whisked Iphigenia away at the last moment and replaced her with a deer.

**Actaeon**
A hunter who stumbled upon Artemis bathing naked. As punishment, she turned him into a stag, and he was chased down and torn apart by his own hunting dogs.

**Calydonian Boar**
A monstrous boar Artemis sent to ravage Calydon in Aetolia after King Oeneus forgot to include her when making sacrifices to the gods. It was killed in the famous Calydonian Boar Hunt led by Oeneus's son Meleager and featuring the huntress Atalanta.

**Niobe's children**
Queen Niobe boasted that she was superior to Leto because she had fourteen children while Leto had only two. Artemis and Apollo killed all of them, with Artemis typically shooting the daughters and Apollo the sons, and the grieving Niobe turned to stone.

**Otus and Ephialtes (the Aloadae)**
Two giant sons of Poseidon who grew enormously each year and plotted to storm Olympus, wanting Artemis and Hera as brides. Artemis turned into a deer and darted between them, so that when they threw their javelins at her they killed each other.

**Leto and Delos**
Artemis and her twin Apollo were born to Leto and Zeus. Hera forbade Leto from giving birth on any land, so she delivered them on the floating island of Delos; Artemis was born first and immediately helped her mother deliver Apollo, which is why she was linked to childbirth.

**Tityos**
A giant who tried to assault Leto, who had earlier been pursued by the serpent Python at Hera's command. Artemis and Apollo shot him down, and he was punished in Tartarus by vultures eating his liver.

**Callisto**
A nymph in Artemis's band of virgin huntresses who was seduced by Zeus and bore a son, Arcas. She was turned into a bear (by Artemis, Hera, or Zeus depending on the version) and later placed in the sky as the constellation Ursa Major.

**Brauron and "playing the bear"**
Artemis's cult site in Attica, said to have been founded by Iphigenia. Young Athenian girls served Artemis there by "playing the bear" (the arkteia) before marriage, since the bear was her sacred animal, and girls dedicated their toys to her before marrying.

**Orion**
The giant hunter, sometimes called the only man Artemis loved. In one version Apollo tricked her into shooting at a distant dot in the sea, which turned out to be Orion swimming; in others she killed him with a scorpion or for attempting to assault her.

**Admetus and Alcestis**
Apollo helped King Admetus meet Pelias's challenge of yoking a lion and a boar to a chariot to win Alcestis's hand. At the wedding Admetus forgot to sacrifice to Artemis, who filled his bridal chamber with snakes until Apollo appeased her.

**Chione**
A woman who bore children to both Hermes and Apollo and then boasted that she was more beautiful than Artemis. Artemis shot her through the tongue with an arrow.

**Adonis and Hippolytus**
Hippolytus, a chaste devotee of Artemis, died because of Aphrodite's scheming. In some myths Artemis avenged him by sending the boar that killed Aphrodite's beloved Adonis.

**Artemis Orthia**
A sanctuary of Artemis at Sparta where, as a rite of passage, Spartan boys were ritually flogged at her altar (the diamastigosis) in an endurance contest.

**Lake Nemi and Ephesus**
Lake Nemi in Italy, called "Diana's Mirror," held a sacred grove of Diana ruled by a priest-king (the rex Nemorensis) who gained the post by killing his predecessor, the subject of the opening of Frazer's The Golden Bough. In the Book of Acts, Paul's preaching in Ephesus angered the silversmith Demetrius and others who made silver shrines of Artemis, whose temple there was a Wonder of the Ancient World.
